title: First powered aeroplane fatality
place: Fort Myer, Virginia, United States
summary: Orville Wright was demonstrating his aeroplane to the United States Army with Lieutenant Thomas Selfridge as his passenger. A propeller cracked and the aeroplane dived into the ground. Orville was badly hurt but recovered, and Selfridge became the first person to die in a powered aeroplane accident.
cause: A split propeller hit a bracing wire, which pulled the rudder out of position and the pilot lost control.
lesson: The accident showed how important head protection was, and early military pilots began wearing helmets. It also pushed the Wright brothers to strengthen their propellers.

title: Amelia Earhart disappearance
place: Pacific Ocean, near Howland Island
summary: Amelia Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan were trying to fly all the way around the world near the equator. On the hardest leg, from New Guinea to tiny Howland Island in the Pacific, they lost radio contact and were never found. A huge search by the United States Navy and Coast Guard found no trace.
cause: Nobody knows for sure. The most widely accepted idea is that they could not find the small island, ran low on fuel and came down in the ocean.
lesson: Her flight showed how hard long-distance navigation over the ocean was, and how much pilots depended on good radio communication. Better radio navigation aids and procedures later made ocean crossings far safer.

title: Comet over Elba
place: Mediterranean Sea, off the island of Elba, Italy
summary: The Comet was the world's first jet airliner. Soon after leaving Rome on a flight from Singapore to London, it broke up at high altitude and fell into the sea near Elba. Nobody on board survived.
cause: Engineers tested a Comet in a giant water tank and found that metal fatigue had caused cracks to grow from the corners of openings in the cabin roof, until the cabin suddenly split open.
lesson: Aeroplanes are now designed and tested to resist metal fatigue, and windows and openings have rounded corners. The Comet investigation became a model for how accidents are studied today.

title: Grand Canyon mid-air collision
place: Grand Canyon, Arizona, United States
aircraft: Lockheed L-1049 Super Constellation and Douglas DC-7
operator: Trans World Airlines and United Air Lines
summary: Two airliners that had left Los Angeles a few minutes apart collided in the sky over the Grand Canyon. Both aeroplanes crashed into the canyon and nobody survived.
cause: Outside the main airways the pilots had to see and avoid each other themselves, with no radar watching them. Clouds and the limited view from the cockpits meant they did not see each other in time.
lesson: This accident led to the Federal Aviation Act of 1958, which created the agency now called the Federal Aviation Administration. Radar air traffic control was expanded across the United States so controllers could keep aeroplanes apart.

title: Munich air disaster
place: Munich-Riem Airport, Munich, West Germany
summary: The aeroplane was carrying the Manchester United football team home from a European Cup match. After two take-off attempts were abandoned, the third attempt failed and the aeroplane ran off the end of a snowy runway. Twenty-three people died, including eight players, and twenty-one survived.
cause: Slush on the runway slowed the aeroplane so much that it could not reach flying speed. The captain was at first blamed for ice on the wings, but a later inquiry cleared him.
lesson: The accident showed how dangerous slush and standing water on runways are. Rules were brought in for measuring runway conditions and for how much slush is allowed before an aeroplane can take off.

title: The Day the Music Died
place: Grant Township, near Clear Lake, Iowa, United States
summary: Rock and roll stars Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and The Big Bopper chartered a small aeroplane to their next concert after a show in Clear Lake, Iowa. It crashed into a farm field a few minutes after take-off on a snowy night. The pilot and all three musicians died.
cause: Investigators found the young pilot was not qualified to fly using instruments alone and flew into poor weather at night. He may also have misread an unfamiliar type of attitude instrument.
lesson: The accident is often used to show why pilots need instrument training before flying at night or in cloud. Weather briefings for pilots were also improved.

title: XB-70 mid-air collision
place: North of Barstow, California, United States
aircraft: North American XB-70 Valkyrie and Lockheed F-104 Starfighter
operator: United States Air Force and NASA
summary: The giant XB-70 Valkyrie was flying in close formation with four other aircraft for a publicity photo. A small F-104 jet drifted into its wing and struck its tail. Both aircraft crashed, and XB-70 pilot Alvin White escaped in his ejection capsule and survived.
cause: The aircraft were flying very close together, and the swirling air around the XB-70's huge wingtip is thought to have pulled the F-104 into it.
lesson: The accident led to much stricter rules for formation flying and photo flights involving test aircraft.

title: X-15 Flight 3-65-97
place: Near Randsburg, California, United States
operator: NASA and United States Air Force
summary: The X-15 rocket plane flew to the edge of space, more than 80 kilometres high. On the way down it went into a spin at very high speed and broke apart. Pilot Michael Adams died, the only death in the X-15 program.
cause: An electrical problem distracted the pilot, and he likely became confused about which way the aircraft was pointing. The control system then could not stop the spin.
lesson: Later research aircraft and spacecraft were given clearer displays showing the pilot which way the craft is heading, and better automatic control systems.

title: Miracle of the Andes
place: Andes mountains, Mendoza Province, Argentina, near the Chilean border
summary: The aeroplane was carrying a rugby team and their friends and family from Uruguay to Chile when it struck a mountain in the high Andes. The survivors sheltered in the snow for 72 days. Two of them, Nando Parrado and Roberto Canessa, walked for ten days across the mountains to find help, and sixteen people were rescued.
cause: The crew thought they had already crossed the mountains and began descending too early while flying in cloud.
lesson: The rescue showed the importance of being able to find a crash site quickly. Modern aircraft carry automatic emergency beacons that send their location to search teams.

title: Eastern Air Lines Flight 401
place: Florida Everglades, near Miami, United States
summary: While approaching Miami at night, the whole flight crew became busy checking a landing gear warning light. Nobody noticed the autopilot had been bumped off and the aeroplane slowly descended into the Everglades swamp. Rescuers in airboats helped 75 survivors.
cause: The crew were all focused on a burnt-out light bulb and did not monitor the aircraft's height.
lesson: This accident helped create Crew Resource Management, training that teaches pilots to share tasks and make sure someone is always flying and watching the aeroplane.

title: Tu-144 Paris Air Show crash
place: Goussainville, near Paris, France
summary: The Soviet supersonic Tu-144 was flying a display at the Paris Air Show. After a steep climb it dived, broke apart in the air and crashed into the village of Goussainville. The six crew and eight people on the ground died.
cause: The official cause was never clearly found. One idea is that the pilots made a sudden manoeuvre to avoid a French photography aircraft.
lesson: Air shows brought in stricter rules about where display aircraft can fly and how far they must stay from crowds and towns.
wikipedia: 1973 Paris Air Show Tupolev Tu-144 crash

title: Turkish Airlines Flight 981
place: Ermenonville Forest, near Paris, France
summary: Shortly after take-off from Paris, a rear cargo door burst open. The sudden loss of air pressure collapsed part of the cabin floor and damaged the control cables. The aeroplane crashed in a forest and nobody survived.
cause: The cargo door latch design made it possible for the door to seem locked when it was not. A similar problem had happened two years earlier on another DC-10.
lesson: DC-10 cargo doors were redesigned, and aircraft floors were strengthened or given vents so a sudden loss of pressure cannot damage the controls.

title: Tenerife airport disaster
place: Los Rodeos Airport, Tenerife, Canary Islands, Spain
summary: Many flights were diverted to the small Los Rodeos airport after an incident at another airport. In thick fog, a KLM 747 began its take-off while a Pan Am 747 was still on the same runway. It is the deadliest accident in aviation history, and 61 people on the Pan Am aeroplane survived.
cause: The KLM captain started the take-off without clearance. Radio calls were blocked and some words were misunderstood in the fog.
lesson: Air traffic control now uses strict standard phrases, and the word take-off is only used when giving clearance. Crew Resource Management training encourages every crew member to speak up if something seems wrong.

title: American Airlines Flight 191
place: Des Plaines, near O'Hare Airport, Chicago, United States
summary: As the DC-10 took off from Chicago, its left engine broke away from the wing. The aeroplane rolled over and crashed in a field near the airport, and nobody on board survived.
cause: Mechanics had used a forklift shortcut to remove and refit the engine, which cracked its mounting. When the engine fell off it also cut hydraulic lines that held the wing slats out.
lesson: Maintenance had to follow the manufacturer's approved methods exactly. Aircraft systems were changed so that slats stay in position even if hydraulics are lost.

title: Air Florida Flight 90
place: 14th Street Bridge, Potomac River, Washington, D.C., United States
summary: On a snowy afternoon, a Boeing 737 struggled to climb after take-off, hit a bridge and fell into the icy Potomac River. Five people on board survived. Bystanders and a park police helicopter crew helped pull them from the water.
cause: The crew did not turn on the engine anti-ice, so a sensor gave false readings and the engines produced less power than shown. Snow and ice on the wings also reduced lift.
lesson: Rules for de-icing aeroplanes and for how long they can wait before take-off in snow became much stricter. Pilot training on icing was improved.

title: British Airways Flight 9
place: Over Mount Galunggung, West Java, Indonesia
summary: At night over Indonesia, the 747 flew into an invisible cloud of volcanic ash from Mount Galunggung and all four engines stopped. The aeroplane glided for about 13 minutes while the crew kept trying to restart the engines. The engines came back to life and everyone landed safely in Jakarta.
cause: Volcanic ash melted inside the hot engines and clogged them. The ash could not be seen on the weather radar at night.
lesson: Volcanic Ash Advisory Centres were set up around the world to track ash clouds and warn pilots so aeroplanes can fly around them.

title: Air Canada Flight 797
place: Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport, Kentucky, United States
summary: A fire started in the rear toilet during the flight and smoke filled the cabin. The pilots made an emergency landing at Cincinnati, and 23 people escaped, but 23 others could not get out in time.
cause: The fire started in or near the rear toilet. The exact source was never confirmed, and it spread out of sight behind the walls.
lesson: Smoke detectors and automatic fire extinguishers were required in aeroplane toilets. Lights along the floor to guide people to the exits and fire-resistant seat covers were added to airliners.

title: Gimli Glider
place: Gimli, Manitoba, Canada
summary: Halfway through a flight from Montreal to Edmonton, a new Boeing 767 ran out of fuel and both engines stopped. Captain Bob Pearson, an experienced glider pilot, glided the aeroplane to a former air force base at Gimli. Everyone survived.
cause: Canada was changing to the metric system, and the fuel was worked out in pounds instead of kilograms, so the aeroplane had less than half the fuel it needed. A faulty fuel gauge also meant the crew could not check.
lesson: Airlines tightened their fuel calculation and checking procedures, and the mix-up showed how important it is to use the same units everywhere.

title: Japan Air Lines Flight 123
place: Mount Takamagahara, Ueno, Gunma Prefecture, Japan
summary: Twelve minutes after leaving Tokyo, the rear pressure wall of the 747 failed and damaged the tail and all the hydraulic systems. The pilots struggled for 32 minutes to control the aeroplane using only engine power before it struck a mountain. Four passengers were rescued the next day. It is the deadliest single-aircraft accident in history.
cause: A repair to the rear pressure bulkhead after an earlier tail strike had been done incorrectly, which let metal fatigue cracks grow.
lesson: Repair inspections became stricter, and aircraft were designed so a failure in the pressure wall cannot drain every hydraulic system. Japan Airlines opened a Safety Promotion Center to teach its staff about the accident.

title: Aloha Airlines Flight 243
place: In flight near Maui, Hawaii, United States
summary: On a short island hop in Hawaii, a large section of the cabin roof tore away at about 7,300 metres. The pilots landed safely at Kahului on Maui. Sadly one flight attendant was lost, but everyone else survived.
cause: The aeroplane had made a very large number of short flights in salty air. Corrosion and metal fatigue had weakened the joints in its skin and inspections did not find the damage.
lesson: The Federal Aviation Administration started an aging aircraft program with much more detailed inspections for older aeroplanes.

title: Kegworth air disaster
place: Near East Midlands Airport, Kegworth, England, United Kingdom
summary: One engine on a nearly new Boeing 737 failed while it was climbing. The pilots shut down the wrong engine and the aeroplane lost power just short of the runway, coming down beside a motorway. Seventy-nine people survived.
cause: The crew misread which engine had the fault. Cabin crew and passengers could see flames from the left engine, but this was not passed on to the pilots.
lesson: Engine instruments were made clearer and pilots were given more training on new aircraft types. Research from this accident improved the brace position and seat strength, and cabin crew are encouraged to tell pilots what they see.

title: United Airlines Flight 232
place: Sioux Gateway Airport, Sioux City, Iowa, United States
summary: The tail engine of the DC-10 broke apart and its pieces cut through all three hydraulic systems, so the normal controls stopped working. The crew, helped by a training pilot travelling as a passenger, steered by changing the power of the two wing engines. The aeroplane crash landed at Sioux City and 184 people survived thanks to their teamwork and a well-prepared rescue team.
cause: A hidden flaw made at the factory in a fan disc inside the engine had grown into a crack that was missed during inspection.
lesson: Engine parts are now inspected with better methods, and aircraft were changed so damage cannot drain all hydraulic systems. The crew's teamwork is still used to teach Crew Resource Management.

title: British Airways Flight 5390
place: Over Didcot, Oxfordshire, England, United Kingdom
summary: As the aeroplane climbed out of Birmingham, a cockpit windscreen blew out and Captain Tim Lancaster was pulled partly out of the window. Cabin crew held onto him while the co-pilot landed safely at Southampton. The captain recovered and everyone survived.
cause: The windscreen had been fitted the day before using bolts that were very slightly too small.
lesson: Maintenance rules were tightened so engineers must check they are using exactly the right parts and have safety-critical work double-checked.

title: Scandinavian Airlines Flight 751
place: Gottröra, near Stockholm, Sweden
summary: Clear ice broke off the wings during take-off from Stockholm and was sucked into both rear engines, which then failed. The pilots glided the aeroplane into a snowy field, where it broke into three pieces. Everyone survived.
cause: The ice on top of the wings had not been found or removed before take-off. An automatic system the pilots had not been told about also pushed the damaged engines to more power.
lesson: De-icing checks became more thorough, including touching the wing surfaces to feel for clear ice. Airlines also made sure pilots were trained on all automatic systems.

title: TWA Flight 800
place: Atlantic Ocean, near East Moriches, New York, United States
summary: Twelve minutes after leaving New York for Paris, the 747 broke apart over the Atlantic Ocean. Nobody survived. Investigators recovered most of the aeroplane from the sea and rebuilt it in a hangar to study it.
cause: Fuel vapour in the nearly empty centre fuel tank exploded, most likely set off by a spark from damaged wiring.
lesson: New rules require airliners to reduce the chance of fuel tank explosions, for example by filling tanks with nitrogen-rich air that will not burn. Wiring inspections were improved.

title: Swissair Flight 111
place: Atlantic Ocean, off Peggys Cove, Nova Scotia, Canada
summary: Soon after leaving New York for Geneva, the crew smelled smoke in the cockpit and began diverting to Halifax. A fire spread above the ceiling and the aeroplane crashed into the ocean near Peggys Cove. Nobody survived.
cause: Wiring for the in-flight entertainment system probably caused a spark, and insulation material behind the walls caught fire and spread it.
lesson: Flammable insulation was replaced across many airliners, and fire tests for aircraft materials became much stricter. Crews were also trained to land as soon as possible when there is smoke.

title: Concorde crash at Paris
place: Gonesse, near Paris, France
summary: During take-off from Paris, Concorde ran over a small metal strip that had fallen from another aircraft. A tyre burst and pieces hit a fuel tank, starting a fire. The aeroplane crashed into a hotel at Gonesse and nobody on board survived.
cause: The metal strip had fallen off a DC-10 that took off a few minutes earlier. The burst tyre caused a shock wave that ruptured the fuel tank.
lesson: Concorde was given Kevlar linings in its fuel tanks and stronger tyres before flying again. Airports also improved runway checks for debris.

title: Air Transat Flight 236
place: Lajes Air Base, Terceira Island, Azores, Portugal
summary: Over the Atlantic Ocean, the Airbus A330 ran out of fuel and both engines stopped. The pilots glided for about 19 minutes and more than 100 kilometres to an air base in the Azores. It is the longest glide by a passenger jet and everyone survived.
cause: A wrong part fitted to the right engine rubbed against a fuel line until it cracked. The crew did not realise there was a leak and moved fuel towards it.
lesson: Airbus added warnings and checklists to help pilots spot fuel leaks. Maintenance rules for using the correct parts were tightened.

title: Air France Flight 358
place: Toronto Pearson International Airport, Ontario, Canada
summary: The Airbus A340 landed in a heavy thunderstorm, ran off the end of the runway and slid into a ravine, where it caught fire. The cabin crew got all the passengers out in about two minutes, and everyone survived.
cause: The aeroplane landed too far along a wet runway with a tailwind, and the crew could not stop in time.
lesson: Canada was urged to add longer safety areas at the ends of runways. Pilots received better guidance on landing in storms, and the fast evacuation showed why passengers should listen to the safety briefing.

title: British Airways Flight 38
place: Heathrow Airport, London, England, United Kingdom
summary: As the Boeing 777 approached Heathrow after a flight from Beijing, both engines lost power. The crew stretched the glide over houses and roads and landed on the grass just short of the runway. Everyone survived.
cause: Ice crystals that had formed in the very cold fuel built up in a part of the fuel system called the fuel-oil heat exchanger and blocked the fuel flow.
lesson: Rolls-Royce redesigned the fuel-oil heat exchanger on its Trent 800 engines so ice could not block it.

title: Miracle on the Hudson
place: Hudson River, New York City, United States
summary: Minutes after take-off from LaGuardia Airport, the Airbus A320 flew into a flock of Canada geese and both engines lost power. Captain Chesley Sullenberger and First Officer Jeffrey Skiles landed on the Hudson River. Ferries and rescue boats picked everyone up and all 155 people survived.
cause: Bird strikes damaged both engines so badly that they could not produce enough power.
lesson: Engine bird strike tests and wildlife management near airports were reviewed. Training for water landings and for losing both engines at low height was improved.

title: Colgan Air Flight 3407
place: Clarence Center, near Buffalo, New York, United States
summary: On a winter night approach to Buffalo, the Q400 slowed down too much and its stall warning activated. The aeroplane crashed into a house, and nobody on board survived.
cause: The captain reacted to the stall warning in the wrong way. Tiredness and gaps in the crew's training also played a part.
lesson: The United States brought in tougher rules for airline pilots, including more flying experience before joining an airline, better stall training and new rest rules to fight tiredness.

title: Air France Flight 447
place: South Atlantic Ocean, between Brazil and Senegal
summary: Flying overnight from Rio de Janeiro to Paris, the Airbus A330 disappeared over the Atlantic Ocean. Some wreckage was found within days, but the flight recorders were not found on the deep sea floor until almost two years later. Nobody survived.
cause: Ice crystals blocked the speed sensors, the autopilot switched off and the pilots did not recognise that the aeroplane had stalled.
lesson: Speed sensors were replaced with better models, and pilots worldwide now practise recovering from stalls and unusual situations at high altitude. New ways of finding flight recorders in deep water were also developed.

title: Asiana Airlines Flight 214
place: San Francisco International Airport, California, United States
summary: Landing at San Francisco on a clear day, the Boeing 777 came in too low and slow and its tail hit the sea wall before the runway. The aeroplane slid along the ground and caught fire. Most people got out quickly, and 304 of the 307 people on board survived.
cause: The pilots did not manage the approach well and misunderstood how the automatic power system would behave, so the aeroplane slowed down too much.
lesson: Airlines put more focus on hand flying skills and on understanding automatic systems. The high survival rate also showed the value of strong seats and well trained cabin crew.

title: Malaysia Airlines Flight 370
place: Southern Indian Ocean, approximate search area west of Australia
summary: The Boeing 777 disappeared from radar on a night flight from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing. Satellite signals showed it kept flying for hours, probably ending far out in the southern Indian Ocean. Australia led an underwater search covering about 120,000 square kilometres, and some pieces of the aeroplane later washed up on islands and coasts near Africa.
cause: Unknown. The main wreckage has not been found, so investigators could not work out why the aeroplane turned off course.
lesson: Airliners are now required to report their position more often over remote oceans, and newer aircraft must be able to send out their location when in distress. Flight recorder location beacons now last longer.

title: SpaceShipTwo VSS Enterprise
place: Mojave Desert, near Cantil, California, United States
summary: During a powered test flight, the SpaceShipTwo spaceplane broke apart high over the Mojave Desert. Co-pilot Michael Alsbury died. Pilot Peter Siebold was thrown clear, his parachute opened and he survived.
cause: The co-pilot unlocked the tail feather system too early, and air forces then pushed it open at the wrong time. The design did not protect against this single mistake.
lesson: Virgin Galactic added a lock that stops the feather system being unlocked too early. Investigators also asked for stronger safety reviews of commercial spaceflight designs.

title: Lion Air Flight 610
place: Java Sea, off Karawang, Indonesia
summary: Minutes after leaving Jakarta, the new Boeing 737 MAX kept pointing its nose down while the pilots fought to climb. The aeroplane crashed into the Java Sea and nobody survived.
cause: A faulty sensor fed wrong information to new flight software called MCAS, which repeatedly pushed the nose down. Pilots had not been told about the system.
lesson: After a second similar accident, the 737 MAX was grounded worldwide for about 20 months. The software was redesigned to use two sensors and pilot training was updated.

title: Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302
place: Near Bishoftu, Ethiopia
summary: Six minutes after taking off from Addis Ababa, a Boeing 737 MAX crashed in a field and nobody survived. It was the second 737 MAX accident in less than five months.
cause: As with Lion Air Flight 610, a faulty sensor caused the MCAS software to repeatedly push the nose down.
lesson: Countries around the world grounded the 737 MAX. It returned to service only after its software was fixed and pilots were retrained, and aircraft certification rules were tightened.

title: Haneda runway collision
place: Haneda Airport, Tokyo, Japan
aircraft: Airbus A350-900 and De Havilland Canada Dash 8
operator: Japan Airlines and Japan Coast Guard
summary: A Japan Airlines A350 landing at Haneda collided with a Coast Guard aircraft that was on the runway, preparing to carry supplies to earthquake survivors. The A350 caught fire, but the cabin crew got all 379 passengers and crew out safely. Five of the six Coast Guard crew died.
cause: Investigators found the Coast Guard crew believed they had permission to enter the runway when they did not, and the mistake was not picked up in time. The final report is still pending.
lesson: Japan added extra controllers and warning systems to watch runways. Airlines around the world pointed to the calm evacuation, where nobody took their bags, as an example to follow.

title: Alaska Airlines Flight 1282
place: In flight over Portland, Oregon, United States
summary: Shortly after take-off from Portland, a panel called a door plug blew out of the side of the cabin. The pilots returned safely to Portland. The two seats next to the panel were empty, and everyone survived with only minor injuries.
cause: Investigators found the four bolts that hold the door plug in place had not been put back after work at the Boeing factory.
lesson: Similar aircraft were grounded for inspections, and the Federal Aviation Administration greatly increased its checks of Boeing's factory work.

title: Jeju Air Flight 2216
place: Muan International Airport, South Korea
summary: Returning from Bangkok, the Boeing 737 hit a flock of birds as it approached Muan. The crew made a second approach and landed without the wheels down, sliding off the runway into a solid mound that held landing equipment. Two cabin crew at the back were rescued.
cause: The final report is still pending. Investigators are looking at the bird strike, which engine was shut down, why the wheels were not lowered and the solid mound at the end of the runway.
lesson: South Korea began rebuilding solid structures near the ends of runways at several airports so they would break away if hit. Bird control at airports is also being reviewed.

title: Potomac River mid-air collision
place: Potomac River, Washington, D.C., United States
aircraft: Bombardier CRJ700 and Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk
operator: PSA Airlines for American Eagle, and United States Army
summary: An airliner coming in to land at Reagan National Airport at night collided with an Army helicopter on a training flight over the Potomac River. Both aircraft fell into the river and nobody survived.
cause: The NTSB final report in 2026 found the main cause was a helicopter route placed too close to the runway approach path, along with weak oversight and too much reliance on pilots seeing each other.
lesson: Helicopter routes near the airport were closed or changed, and flights near busy airports now rely more on controllers and electronic systems that show where other aircraft are.

title: Delta Connection Flight 4819
place: Toronto Pearson International Airport, Ontario, Canada
summary: In gusty winter winds, the CRJ900 landed hard at Toronto, lost a wing and flipped upside down on the snowy runway. Passengers hung in their seatbelts and then climbed out, and rescue crews arrived within moments. Everyone survived.
cause: The final report is still pending. Early findings show a hard landing broke part of the landing gear.
lesson: The accident showed how strong modern seats, seatbelts and fast airport rescue teams help people survive. Further lessons will come from the final report.

title: Air India Flight 171
place: Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India
summary: Seconds after taking off from Ahmedabad for London, the Boeing 787 lost power and came down on buildings of a medical college. One passenger survived. It was the first fatal accident involving a 787.
cause: The final report is still pending. A preliminary report found the switches that send fuel to both engines moved to the off position just after take-off, but why this happened has not been officially explained.
lesson: Airlines in India and elsewhere checked the fuel control switches on their aircraft. More lessons are expected when the final report is published.
